passage:
Monday. In the sprint review the dashboard broke. Jaya, the team lead, said, “That was my call to skip testing. I'm sorry. Let's fix it together.” Rehana, three months into the job, had never heard a boss say that.

Thursday. The client praised the launch. Jaya said, “That was Ketan's idea and Meera's late nights. I just signed the emails.” Ketan sat up straighter, and Meera looked at her notes and smiled.

The next Tuesday, before choosing a new tool, Jaya asked, “Rehana, you've used both. What do you think?” Rehana's heart thumped. She answered, and Jaya wrote it down.

That night Rehana noticed she had never once feared Jaya's mood, and trusted every instruction more for it.

qa.q: What did Jaya say when the dashboard broke?
qa.a: Jaya said, “That was my call to skip testing. I'm sorry. Let's fix it together.”

qa.q: What was Rehana feeling when Jaya asked what Rehana thought about the tools?
qa.a: Rehana felt nervous but valued, since a leader asked someone three months into the job for a view and wrote the answer down.

qa.q: What choice did Jaya make when the client praised the launch?
qa.a: Jaya credited Ketan's idea and Meera's late nights instead of taking the credit.

qa.q: What might Jaya be feeling when saying sorry in front of the team?
qa.a: Jaya may feel exposed but secure enough to admit the error, trusting that honesty earns more respect than pretending.

grounding: A newcomer watches a leader who admits mistakes, gives credit and asks for views, and comes to trust the leader more.

passage:
Saurabh, since you've just got your first team, listen to this. I'm Rafiq. At twenty-four I was the junior in Devraj sir's office. In my second week he sent a wrong figure to head office, and the next morning he told the whole room, “I got it wrong, and I'm sorry. Rafiq caught it.” I hadn't caught it, exactly; I had only asked a question. He gave me the credit anyway.

Every week he asked each of us, “What am I missing?” He listened even to the peon. When the company changed hands, half the office followed Devraj sir to his new firm. Nobody followed the new manager, who sat behind a closed door and signed papers. I've thought about that ever since.

qa.q: What did Devraj sir say the morning after sending the wrong figure?
qa.a: Devraj sir said, “I got it wrong, and I'm sorry. Rafiq caught it.”

qa.q: Why might Rafiq have remembered that morning for so long?
qa.a: Rafiq had never seen a senior person admit a mistake and share credit, so it left a trust and respect that lasted.

qa.q: What did Devraj sir do each week that showed he wanted the team's views?
qa.a: Devraj sir asked each person, “What am I missing?” and listened even to the peon.

qa.q: How might the peon have felt when asked, “What am I missing?”
qa.a: The peon probably felt surprised and respected, unused to being asked for a view.

grounding: An elder recalls a leader who admitted mistakes, gave credit and asked for views, and whom people followed by trust rather than position.

passage:
The flood relief camp in the school building had power for only two hours a day, and three trucks were due before dark. Kamal, three weeks into his first job with the NGO, watched Ishita, the camp head, run the evening meeting by lantern light.
“First, my mistake,” she said. “I counted the rice sacks wrong yesterday. We're short by twenty. That's on me.” Nobody had expected that.
Then she turned to the volunteers. “Rekha found the dry storeroom. Salim fixed the pump. Thank you both.” Rekha looked at the floor, smiling.
“Now, what am I missing? Tell me.” Three people spoke at once.
Kamal noticed the older volunteers stayed late for her without being asked. He wrote in his notebook: trust, not title.

qa.q: By how many sacks was the rice short?
qa.a: The rice was short by twenty sacks.

qa.q: What was Kamal feeling as he watched Ishita run the meeting?
qa.a: He felt surprised and admiring, noticing how her honesty and credit-giving made people trust her.

qa.q: What does Ishita do that makes people want to follow her?
qa.a: She admits her own mistake, gives specific credit to volunteers and asks for views, so people trust her rather than just obey.

qa.q: How might Rekha have felt when Ishita thanked her?
qa.a: Rekha seemed shy but pleased, smiling at the floor at being noticed in front of everyone.

grounding: Shows a junior watching a leader admit mistakes, give credit and ask for views under pressure, and learning trust outlasts position.

passage:
In the bank branch in Jayanagar, Dolma had been an officer for six months when the big client meeting went wrong. The loan papers had the wrong interest date.
Deepak, the branch manager, didn't look at her, though she had prepared the file. He said to the client, “That's my error. I signed it without checking. We'll correct it today.”
After the client left, he called the team together. “Dolma found the fix in ten minutes. Good work.” Then he asked, “What should we change so this doesn't happen again?” Dolma suggested a second check. He wrote it on the board.
That evening Dolma thought about her old manager, who had shouted at juniors in front of clients. Nobody had stayed late for him. Everyone stayed for Deepak.

qa.q: What was wrong in the loan papers?
qa.a: They had the wrong interest date.

qa.q: How did Dolma feel when Deepak took the blame in front of the client?
qa.a: She felt relieved and grateful, and grew to respect and trust him.

qa.q: What can a new leader learn from Deepak?
qa.a: Take responsibility in front of others, give specific credit to the team, and ask them how to improve, which builds lasting trust.

qa.q: How might the client have seen Deepak's response?
qa.a: The client probably felt reassured by his honesty and quick promise to fix it.

grounding: Shows a junior watching a manager admit a mistake, give her credit and ask for views, learning that trust outlasts position.

passage:
“Okay, team,” said Pankaj, the night editor, at the newsroom's ten o'clock meeting. “Before we start, yesterday's headline on the water story was wrong. I approved it. My mistake.”
Uma, the youngest reporter, blinked.
“Now, the rail strike piece. Uma, you got the union leader to talk when nobody else could. Great work.”
“Thanks,” Uma managed.
“What are we missing tonight? I want to hear from everyone, especially the new people.”
Imtiaz said, “The hospital story needs a second source.”
“Good. Uma, what do you think?”
Uma swallowed. “Maybe we lead with the strike, not the minister?”
Pankaj nodded slowly. “Yes. Let's do that.”
After the meeting, Uma whispered to Imtiaz, “Is he always like this?” Imtiaz smiled. “That's why nobody leaves.”

qa.q: Who did Uma get to talk for the rail strike piece?
qa.a: The union leader.

qa.q: How did Uma feel when Pankaj asked for her opinion?
qa.a: Uma felt nervous and surprised, swallowing before speaking, but encouraged to share an idea.

qa.q: What makes Pankaj a leader people stay with?
qa.a: He admits his mistakes, gives specific credit and genuinely asks for views, even from the newest people.

qa.q: How does Imtiaz see Pankaj's style?
qa.a: Imtiaz respects it, saying it's the reason nobody leaves the team.

grounding: Shows a junior reporter watching an editor admit a mistake, give credit and ask for views, learning that trust lasts longer than position.

passage:
I'm Sudha, and I've been at the newsroom of a Pune paper for a year. The thing I'll remember is one Tuesday meeting.
Gargi, our editor, walked in and said, "Before anything else: yesterday's flood headline was my call, and it was wrong. The numbers were from the old report. I've sent the correction." Nobody had to hunt for a culprit.
Then she said Rohit's photo had carried the whole front page, and asked me, the most junior person there, what readers in my area were talking about. I stammered through something about water tankers. She wrote it on the board.
My old boss at a magazine had a bigger title and a louder voice, and we did what he said because we had to. With Gargi, people stay late because they want to. I didn't understand the difference until I watched it.

qa.q: What did Gargi say was wrong with the flood headline?
qa.a: The numbers were from the old report.

qa.q: How did Sudha feel being asked for a view in the meeting?
qa.a: Sudha felt nervous, stammering through the answer, but also valued when Gargi wrote it on the board.

qa.q: What could Sudha take from Gargi's style for the future?
qa.a: Own mistakes openly, give specific credit and ask the quietest people for their view; that builds trust a title alone cannot.

qa.q: How might Rohit feel hearing Gargi credit the photo in front of everyone?
qa.a: Rohit probably felt proud and noticed, which makes the extra effort feel worthwhile.

grounding: Shows a junior watching a leader who admits a mistake, credits others and asks for views, and learning that trust outlasts positional authority.
